newsitem.title: USA: USDA holds conference on HACCP implementation.
newsitem.headline: USDA holds conference on HACCP implementation.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Agriculture Thursday began the first in a series of conferences on implementation of new meat inspection rules announced in July.
The rules, which will revolutionize meat inspection, are to go into effect in stages, with the first stage taking effect in January next year.
"We are seeking input from all interested parties on the best way to carry out these new food safety requirements," said USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service Administrator Michael Taylor.

The two-day meeting starting Thursday, the first of a dozen conferences scheduled to be held between now and April, focused on new requirements for slaughter plants to test for generic E. Coli bacteria.
Under the timetable set in USDA's final regulations, plants must start E. Coli testing in January, in the first wave of implementation of the new rule.
The American Meat Institute (AMI), which represents a large segment of the slaughter and meat processing industry, questioned the testing provisions.
"AMI continues to believe that microbial testing provisions in the proposed rule are inappropriately designed," AMI said in a position paper before the meeting.

"End-product testing and associated performance levels are contrary to HACCP, which focuses on prevention within the process, not detection at the end of the process, to ensure food safety," the paper added.
Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) is the food safety principle on which the new regulations are modeled.
National Meat Association Executive Director Rosemary Mucklow said several parts of the regulation still needed to be clarified.
"We are waiting for our government to tell us how to implement (the regulation)," Mucklow said.
